clue.text: Set with mishap at sea? They hope not!

definitions.text: Set with mishap at sea? They hope not!

indicators.note: at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters of the two words get rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor's worry: being struck by misfortune while out on the ocean is exactly what crew members dread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' is the anagram signal, working on SET and MISHAP. The whole clue also works as the definition, because crewmates on a voyage hope not to meet with a mishap.
explanation.definitionFit: Fellow crew members on a voyage are the people who would dread a disaster on the water.

clue.text: Replace inadequate substitute worker

indicators.note: inadequate means falling short, so the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: to supply can mean to stand in or substitute, as a supply teacher does
a worker ant is the classic crossword worker

explanation.surface: A manager wants to swap out a poor stand-in employee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inadequate' trims SUPPLY to SUPPL; a supply teacher is a British stand-in teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust someone and take their place is to replace them.

clue.text: Phoney person gets nothing right, going after this person's job

indicators.note: going after puts the following letters behind the job word

parts.note: this person is the setter, I, and this person's is read as I am, shortened to I'm
a post is a job or position
O is a zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A fraud who has nothing correct is angling for the setter's position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this person's' is read as 'this person is', I'M. 'going after' puts O and R after IMPOST.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraudster pretending to be someone else is a fake, a phoney person.

clue.text: Indigenous people wander north over island

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above what follows
in a down clue, going north means reading upwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: to roam is to wander

explanation.surface: Native people drift northwards across an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'north' reverses ROAM to MAOR in this down clue; 'over' puts it above IS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Polynesian first inhabitants of New Zealand are an indigenous people.

clue.text: Container that's brown put outside home, third for recycling

indicators.note: the colour word is placed outside, around the other letters

parts.note: tan is a light brown colour
in can mean at home

indicators.note: the third of a word is its third letter, here of recycling

explanation.surface: A brown bin goes outside the house, the third one put out for recycling collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'third for recycling' takes the third letter of that word, not a third bin; 'put outside' wraps the colour around home and that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A metal food can is a container, and the phrase is also used for the empty one.

clue.text: Business guys reconvened en masse, about fifty

indicators.note: about means around, so these letters go around the numeral
reconvened means brought together again in a new arrangement, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A group of businessmen, about fifty strong, meets again all together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reconvened' rearranges the French phrase to SAESMEN, and 'about' wraps that around the Roman numeral for fifty.
explanation.definitionFit: Men who sell goods for a firm are commercial guys, travelling or in shops.

clue.text: Animal with desire has briefly got outside

indicators.note: something that has got outside another surrounds it, so these letters go around the others
briefly means cut short, so the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: taken as written before it is shortened
a yen is a longing or desire

explanation.surface: A creature with a craving has just slipped out of its enclosure for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' trims the S off the first word, and 'got outside' wraps what is left around the longing.
explanation.definitionFit: The laughing scavenger of the African plains is an example of a wild beast.

clue.text: Has to go around smart coastal town

indicators.note: the first word must go around the second, enclosing it

parts.note: to smart is to sting with pain

explanation.surface: A dapper visitor has to tour a seaside resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smart' is the verb, to hurt, not stylish. Hastings is a town on the south coast of England, site of the 1066 battle.
explanation.definitionFit: The East Sussex resort on the English Channel is a seaside town.

clue.text: Does wrong, pocketing copper coin

indicators.note: pocketing means putting inside, so the scrambled letters hold the metal
wrong means not right, so the letters are in a wrong order and get rearranged

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: Someone does wrong by stealing a copper coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' turns DOES into ESDO, which is 'pocketing' CU.
explanation.definitionFit: The former currency unit of Portugal is an example of a coin.

clue.text: A maiden exploited, unlike a famous queen?

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
used means taken advantage of

explanation.surface: A young woman is taken advantage of, a fate no royal would put up with.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Victoria is said to have declared 'We are not amused', so the definition describes the opposite of her.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria's famous reply means she was not entertained, so the opposite is a person tickled and entertained.

clue.text: Dad — gosh! — beginning to nibble cinema food

parts.note: pop is an informal word for a father
cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like gosh

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is taken

explanation.surface: A child exclaims as their father starts munching snacks at the pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: COR is a British exclamation of surprise. 'beginning to' takes the N of 'nibble'.
explanation.definitionFit: Puffed maize kernels are the classic snack eaten while watching a film.

clue.text: Box with crazy old jokes?

parts.note: a chest is a large box for storage
nuts is slang for crazy

explanation.surface: A comedian's routine: a boxful of daft, tired gags.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is the figurative sense, not the tree's fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A stale, overused joke or story is idiomatically called by the name of a roasted autumn nut.

clue.text: Skilled worker is biased, wanting leader got rid of

indicators.note: the word wants its leading letter removed, so the first letter is taken away

parts.note: partisan means prejudiced in favour of one side

explanation.surface: A craftsman is described as prejudiced and keen to sack the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting leader got rid of' drops the P from PARTISAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A craftsperson who works with their hands at a trade is a skilled worker.

clue.text: A new husband in gloomy state — a male condition!

indicators.note: the letters sit in the word for the state of mind, going inside it

parts.note: a mood can mean a sulky or gloomy state of mind
H is a genealogical abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A newlywed man sulking: an exclamation that grumpiness is just how men are.
explanation.walkthrough: A, N and H go in MOOD, after its M.
explanation.definitionFit: The state of being an adult man, with the qualities that go with it, is a male condition.

clue.text: Admit defeat now and then, sir? Oh, that's bad!

indicators.note: bad here signals that the letters are in a poor order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone occasionally concedes, and a companion groans at the sir's poor showing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's bad' is the anagram signal on NOW AND THEN SIR OH, fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from card games, where laying down your cards means giving up, so it means to concede.

clue.text: Exhausted wife, a female joining party in NI

parts.note: W is the genealogical abbreviation for wife
she refers to a female
the DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A tired wife and another woman sign up to a Northern Ireland political party.
explanation.walkthrough: The DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party, a Northern Ireland political party.
explanation.definitionFit: Being finished and no longer effective, all spent, is the informal sense shared with exhausted.

clue.text: Out of sorts titaness can be most unpleasant

indicators.note: out of sorts means not in proper order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grumpy female Titan of myth can be a real horror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of sorts' is the anagram signal on TITANESS.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of nasty means the most disagreeable or unpleasant.

clue.text: A situation where some may be brought down to earth

definitions.text: A situation where some may be brought down to earth

parts.words: A situation where some may be brought down to earth
parts.note: brought down to earth usually means disillusioned, but here it is literal: planes landing

explanation.surface: A place where people get their dreams deflated.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for being humbled hides the literal sense of aircraft landing.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerodrome is a place where aircraft literally come down to land.

clue.text: Little girl with emotional state, extreme suffering

parts.note: Di is a short form of the girl's name Diana
stress is a state of mental tension

explanation.surface: A young girl in an emotional condition is in great pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little girl' is a shortened name, DI, not a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Great anguish or acute pain is extreme suffering.

clue.text: Removes risk element from brilliant exercises

parts.note: def is slang for excellent or brilliant
to exercise a right or skill is to use it

explanation.surface: A trainer praises superb workouts for taking the danger out of fitness.
explanation.walkthrough: DEF is slang for brilliant; 'exercises' is a verb here, not workouts.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a bomb safe by taking out its detonator is to take away its dangerous component.

clue.text: Road held up with animals hidden under covers

indicators.note: in a down clue, the animals sit hidden beneath what comes before
in a down clue, held up means raised, read upwards, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: apes are animals

explanation.surface: Traffic on a road is delayed while creatures shelter beneath blankets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held up' reverses RD to DR in this down clue, and 'hidden under' puts APES below it.
explanation.definitionFit: Curtains or hanging cloths are things that cover windows.

clue.text: Superficial account placed in record folder

indicators.note: placed in means put inside, so the abbreviation goes inside the folder word

parts.note: a file is a folder for keeping records

explanation.surface: An office clerk puts a shallow report in a filing folder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'record folder' is read as one phrase for the container, not as a record plus a folder.
explanation.definitionFit: A glib, shallow argument lacking depth is superficial.

clue.text: Applauds a miser reforming, having hoarded pennies once

indicators.note: hoarding means keeping something stored away inside, so the letters go inside
reforming means taking a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: D stood for pennies in pre-decimal British money, from the Latin denarius

explanation.surface: People praise a skinflint who mends his ways despite having stashed away old coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reforming' turns A MISER into AMIRES, and 'having hoarded' puts D inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To applaud someone is to praise them, and to look up to them with respect is close in sense.

clue.text: A change of policy said to be needed in military action

indicators.note: said to be means spoken, so the phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: a tack is a change of course or approach, so this is a tack

explanation.surface: A general says a new strategy is needed for the coming offensive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said to be' signals a homophone: 'a tack' sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An assault by armed forces on an enemy is a military action.

clue.text: Lots of married fools

parts.note: asses are fools

explanation.surface: Many husbands and wives are idiots.
explanation.definitionFit: Great quantities or heaps of something are lots.

clue.text: One can work a miracle? The claim's false!

indicators.note: a false arrangement of these letters is not the real one, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sceptic hears that someone performs miracles and dismisses the boast as untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'false' is the anagram signal on THE CLAIM'S.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval practitioner who claimed to turn base metals into gold was attempting a kind of miracle.

clue.text: Severe sort of wind heading for England

parts.note: the auster is the south wind, named by the Romans

indicators.note: a heading is the top of something, so the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A harsh gale is blowing towards England.
explanation.walkthrough: AUSTER is the old poetic name for the south wind; 'heading for' gives E from England.
explanation.definitionFit: Stern, strict and unadorned are all shades of meaning shared with severe.

clue.text: Most of cast starts to experience pressure — docile types?

indicators.note: most of a word is all of it except the end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: to cast off skin is to shed it

indicators.note: the starts of the two words are their opening letters

explanation.surface: Most of a theatre company begins to feel the strain, leaving a meek bunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' is a verb here, as a snake casts its skin: SHED, cut to SHE by 'Most of'. 'starts to' takes E and P.
explanation.definitionFit: Meek people who follow the crowd are likened to the flock animal, a familiar metaphor for docility.

clue.text: Support one group and tease kids naughtily

indicators.note: acting naughtily means misbehaving, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A playground scene: someone backs one gang and mischievously taunts the children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naughtily' is the anagram signal on TEASE KIDS.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to back one party in a dispute rather than staying neutral.
